meta.title: AI adoption review checklist for Irish hospitals
meta.description: Questions administrators and nurse leaders can ask when a vendor proposes an AI product: purpose, applicable rules, patient data, security and operations.
meta.lead: Use this when you receive a specific proposal. Tick each item when you have a written answer. The items are the author’s list; the checklists and the facts page give the sources behind many of them.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
items: The job the tool will do is described in one sentence and agreed by the department that will use it.
Who will use it, and who will be affected by its output, is listed (including nurses and front-desk staff).
Where the AI enters the process and who makes the final decision are written down.

sections.heading: Rules and regulatory status
items: You have noted whether your hospital is a deployer of the AI system under the EU AI Act and whether the tool is, or may become, high-risk.
The vendor states in writing whether it treats the product as a medical device and which conformity route applies; HPRA does not approve devices, so ask for the CE-marking details.
You have asked who is the provider and whether any in-house development makes your hospital a provider or manufacturer.
You have read HIQA’s national guidance (final text) and noted what it asks of your service.

sections.heading: Patient data
items: The vendor states where data is stored and processed, whether it is re-used, and who is controller and processor.
A data protection impact assessment has been done with your data protection officer before go-live.
The tool does not make decisions about patients solely by automated means without a person who can intervene.
The patient-facing explanation of the tool is agreed.

sections.heading: Security and incidents
items: The incident card lists who reports to HPRA, who tells the vendor, and the 72-hour GDPR clock for personal data breaches.
You know how software updates and field safety notices reach you and who acts on them.
The vendor will tell you promptly about a breach, in writing.

sections.heading: Performance and oversight
items: The vendor’s validation is described in writing, including data sets used and limits.
Someone with competence, training and authority can oversee and override the tool.
Logs under your control are kept for an appropriate period (the AI Act sets at least six months for high-risk systems).

sections.heading: Operations and people
items: Staff who will use the tool are trained before go-live, including its limits (AI literacy).
The tool is on your list of AI tools with a named owner.
An audit or review is scheduled, and workers have been informed where the AI Act requires it.
